pedagogy.summary: A decimal is simply another NAME for a fraction with denominator 10 or 100 — the same quantity, the same point on the number line. 3/10 = 0.3 and 27/100 = 0.27 because the decimal places ARE the tenths and hundredths columns: the first place after the point counts tenths, the second counts hundredths. The load-bearing insight is that the place, not just the digits, carries the denominator — so 7 hundredths needs a placeholder zero (0.07), not 0.7. Teach the two forms as interchangeable labels for one amount, tying each decimal to its fraction and to a single point on a line or a shaded grid, so children never treat 0.3 and 3/10 as different things.
bestPractices: Introduce the decimal as a re-labelling of a tenths/hundredths fraction on the SAME grid or number line — shade 27 of 100 squares and write both 27/100 and 0.27 for the identical picture.

Make the place-value columns explicit: the first place after the point is tenths, the second is hundredths, so the denominator is read off the position; write fractions and decimals side by side in a place-value chart.
Stress the placeholder zero with contrasting pairs — 3/10 = 0.3 but 3/100 = 0.03, and 7/100 = 0.07 not 0.7 — so children attend to place, not just to the digits.
Place 0.3 and 3/10 (and 0.30) at the same point on a number line to establish that the two notations name one quantity, defeating 'a decimal and a fraction are different numbers'.
Read decimals in place-value language ('twenty-seven hundredths', 'three tenths') not as 'point two seven', so the fraction meaning stays audible.
keyRepresentations: 10×10 hundredths grid shaded and labelled with both the fraction and the decimal
Place-value chart with tenths and hundredths columns beside the fraction
Number line where 0.3, 0.30 and 3/10 mark the same point
Contrasting pairs 3/10 = 0.3 vs 3/100 = 0.03 to spotlight the placeholder zero
commonMisconceptions: Dropping the placeholder zero — writing 7/100 as 0.7 (or reading 0.07 as 7/10), ignoring that the place fixes the denominator.
Treating a decimal and its fraction as different numbers — not seeing 0.3 and 3/10 as the same quantity at the same point.
Reading the digits after the point as an ordinary whole number ('0.27 means twenty-seven') rather than as 27 hundredths.
Mapping the numerator straight after the point regardless of denominator, so 3/10 and 3/100 both become 0.3.
Thinking annexing a zero changes the value (0.3 vs 0.30 seen as different).

learn.summary: A decimal with one or two decimal places is another name for a fraction with denominator 10 or 100: the same quantity, the same point on the number line (3/10 = 0.3, 27/100 = 0.27). The load-bearing insight is that the PLACE, not just the digits, carries the denominator: the first place after the point counts tenths, the second counts hundredths, so 7 hundredths needs a placeholder zero (0.07), not 0.7. Teach the two forms as interchangeable labels for one amount by tying each decimal to its fraction and to a single point on a line or a shaded grid, so children do not treat 0.3 and 3/10 as different things.

activities.title: Shade, name it twice, and pin one point
feedback: If a learner writes 7/100 as 0.7: ask them to place both 0.7 and their 7 shaded squares (7/100) on the number line. 0.7 lands exactly at seven tenths, far from seven hundredths — the shading contradicts it. Point to the place-value chart: 7 hundredths sits in the SECOND place, so the tenths place needs a 0, giving 0.07.
If a learner says 0.3 and 3/10 are different numbers: place 0.3, 0.30 and 3/10 on the same line and shade the same grid for each — all name one point and one amount, two notations for the same value.

If a learner reads 0.27 as 'twenty-seven': read it aloud as 'twenty-seven hundredths' and locate it on the hundredths grid; the digits are 2 tenths and 7 hundredths, together 27 hundredths, between 0 and 1 — not the whole number 27.
If a learner converts both 3/10 and 3/100 to 0.3: contrast the pair directly — 3/10 = 0.3 but 3/100 = 0.03 — and point to which column the 3 occupies.
activities.rationale: Letting the child control the shading and read off both labels makes the equivalence experienced rather than asserted, and contrasting a wrong placement (0.7) against the shaded 7/100 makes the placeholder's role concrete. Instruction should make the place-value meaning and the placeholder explicit rather than teach a digit-copying rule.
sourceClaims: Children commonly err by drawing false analogies with whole numbers and by mishandling place value in decimal notation; linking fractions and decimals is desirable but is frequently done incorrectly, so instruction must make the place-value meaning (and the role of the placeholder) explicit rather than teaching a digit-copying rule.
learnerActions: On a 10×10 hundredths grid, shade 27 of the 100 squares; write the fraction (27/100) and the decimal (0.27) for the exact same picture, side by side in a place-value chart with tenths and hundredths columns.
Mark where this amount sits on a 0-to-1 number line; confirm 27/100 and 0.27 land on the same single point.
Now shade just 7 squares. Write the fraction (7/100) and decide the decimal. Predict and then check: does it write as 0.7 or 0.07?
Compare where 0.7 would fall on the number line versus where your 7 shaded squares sit — notice 0.7 lands far past 7 hundredths, exactly at seven tenths.
Toggle between 0.3, 0.30 and 3/10 and place each on the number line to confirm all three mark the identical point.
activities.intendedInsight: A decimal and its fraction are one number wearing two names; the place after the point fixes the denominator, so the placeholder zero in 0.07 holds the tenths place empty and is not decoration.

activities.title: Predict then reconcile on the number line
feedback: A prediction of 'different points' reveals the belief that a decimal and a fraction are different numbers; after they coincide on the line, name explicitly that they are two notations for one quantity.
For the 3/100 challenge: 3/100 is three hundredths = 0.03, with a placeholder zero in the tenths place; only 3/10 is 0.3.
activities.rationale: A predict-then-check sequence makes a hidden belief visible and gives the child a contradiction to resolve, which targets the 'decimal and fraction are different numbers' misconception directly rather than merely asserting equivalence.
sourceClaims: Children commonly err by drawing false analogies with whole numbers and by mishandling place value in decimal notation; linking fractions and decimals is desirable but is frequently done incorrectly, so instruction must make the place-value meaning (and the role of the placeholder) explicit rather than teaching a digit-copying rule.
learnerActions: Before locating anything, predict: will 0.3 and 3/10 land at the same point on a number line, at different points, or is one bigger — and WHY?
State your reason aloud or in writing, then place 0.3, 3/10 and 0.30 on a marked line.
Observe that all three coincide; explain how this fits (or revises) your prediction.
Answer a challenge: a friend says 3/10 and 3/100 both write as 0.3 — what would you tell them, and what should 3/100 actually be?
activities.intendedInsight: Committing to a prediction and its reason surfaces whether a child believes a decimal and a fraction are different kinds of number; reconciling with the shared point corrects it.

activities.title: Reference grid with reveal flaps
feedback: Use the 'why the zero?' flap when a learner forgets the placeholder: the zero keeps the tenths place empty so the next digit counts hundredths.
Use the contrasting-pair flap whenever 3/10 and 3/100 are confused.
activities.rationale: A fixed annotated reference communicates the equivalence and placeholder clearly and supports recall, but because the child cannot drive the shading or test a wrong placement it reinforces rather than builds the insight — pair it with the interactive shading task.
learnerActions: Use a static hundredths grid annotated with both notations: tap or lift a flap on a shaded region to reveal 'this shading is 27/100 = 0.27'.
Open a contrasting-pair flap that shows 3/10 = 0.3 beside 3/100 = 0.03, and a 'why the zero in 0.07?' flap.
Consult a number line showing 0.3 = 3/10 sharing one point.
activities.intendedInsight: The equivalence of the two notations and the role of the placeholder zero can be seen at a glance as a reference, reinforcing what was built through shading and prediction.

activities.title: Convert, match and locate (check-up)
feedback: The 7/100 item is the discriminator: a child who copies digits writes 0.7 and reveals the rule is hollow; a child who understands place writes 0.07. Reteach with the place-value chart and grid if 0.7 appears.
A full response explains that a decimal and its fraction name the same quantity at the same point because the places count tenths and hundredths, and handles 3/10 vs 3/100 and 0.3 = 0.30.
activities.rationale: Conversion both ways and equivalence-location are cleanly checkable, and distractors drawn from the placeholder and no-equivalence errors make the check diagnostic. It specifically exposes whether a child is relying on a hollow digit-copying rule. It confirms the output rather than teaching the one-quantity insight, so use it after the building tasks.
sourceClaims: Children commonly err by drawing false analogies with whole numbers and by mishandling place value in decimal notation; linking fractions and decimals is desirable but is frequently done incorrectly, so instruction must make the place-value meaning (and the role of the placeholder) explicit rather than teaching a digit-copying rule.
learnerActions: Write 3/10 and 7/100 as decimals, and write 0.27 as a fraction.
Match a set of fractions to their decimals, including the contrasting pair 3/10 and 3/100.
Choose which value equals 3/10 from options including 0.3 (correct) and 0.03 (tempting but wrong).
Explain in words: is 0.3 the same as 3/10, or different — and how do you know?
activities.intendedInsight: Converting each way, locating equivalents, and justifying equivalence confirms whether the place-value meaning is understood or a hollow digit-copying rule is in use.

constraints: The represented objects are planar (grid, number line, place-value chart); depth carries no meaning here, so flat representations are appropriate and a 3D model adds cost without conceptual gain for this objective.

The static annotated reference grid supports and reinforces but does not let the child drive the shading or test a wrong placement, so it should accompany, not replace, the interactive shading and prediction tasks.

The convert/match/locate check-up assesses the output; on its own it does not build the equivalence insight and can be passed by a digit-copying rule on tenths alone — include the 7/100 item and an explanation question so a hollow rule is exposed.
Read decimals in place-value language ('twenty-seven hundredths', 'three tenths') rather than 'point two seven', so the fraction meaning stays audible.

Treat 0.3 = 0.30 as naming one value: annexing a zero after the last decimal place does not change the amount; distinguish this from the placeholder zero in 0.07, which does change the value by shifting the digit's place.
Recognising and writing decimal equivalents of tenths and hundredths is the stated curriculum objective; the activities serve it but do not themselves prove any one medium is superior.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; the sources were not re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The DfE National Curriculum (Year 4) citation is marked verified:false in the row and states pupils should recognise and write decimal equivalents of tenths/hundredths. It supports the objective/topic, not the pedagogical principle of any activity, so it was removed from activity sourceClaims and is retained here only as curriculum context, unconfirmed.

Self-audit of arithmetic/notation: 27/100 = 0.27, 7/100 = 0.07, 3/100 = 0.03, 3/10 = 0.3, 0.3 = 0.30 all check out; 0.7 = 70/100 (seven tenths) lands far from 7/100 (seven hundredths), supporting the placeholder contrast. No conceptual errors found in the source's worked examples.

The 'try to write 0.7 and the marker jumps far away' contrast is sound provided the number line is scaled 0 to 1 (or beyond) so 0.7 and 0.07 are visibly distinct; ensure the scale makes seven tenths clearly distant from seven hundredths.

assess.poeTask: Before locating anything, ask the child to PREDICT whether 0.3 and 3/10 will land at the same point on a number line, at different points, or whether 0.3 is bigger or smaller — and WHY. The reason is diagnostic: a child predicting different points reveals the decimal-and-fraction-are-different-numbers belief. Then place both (and 0.30) on a marked line: all coincide. Have the child reconcile this with their prediction.
probeDeeper: You wrote 7/100 = 0.07. Why does it need the zero — what would 0.7 mean instead?
Is 0.3 the same as 0.30? How do you know?
Show me 0.27 and 27/100 on this number line — do they land in the same place or different places? Why?
A friend says 3/10 and 3/100 both write as 0.3. What would you tell them, and what should 3/100 be?
assess.correctAnswer: 3/10 = 0.3; 7/100 = 0.07 (with the placeholder zero); 0.27 = 27/100. 0.3 is the same as 3/10 — both are three tenths, the same quantity at the same point on the number line.

errorPatterns.pattern: Drops the placeholder zero — writes 7/100 as 0.7 (or reads 0.07 as 7/10), mapping the numerator straight after the point regardless of the denominator.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Use the place-value chart / hundredths grid to show 7 hundredths sits in the second place, needing a zero in the tenths place; contrast 3/10 = 0.3 with 3/100 = 0.03. Reteach that place fixes the denominator (hundredths).
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Writes 0.7 for 7/100; converts 3/10 and 3/100 to the same decimal.

errorPatterns.pattern: Treats the decimal and the fraction as different numbers — '0.3 and 3/10 aren't the same, one's a decimal and one's a fraction'.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Put 0.3, 0.30 and 3/10 on the same number line and same shaded grid so all name one point/quantity. Reteach that decimal and fraction are two notations for the same value.
errorPatterns.distractor: 0.3 and 3/10 are different numbers — one is a decimal and one is a fraction.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: On tier-2, says they are different, or places 0.3 and 3/10 at different points.

errorPatterns.pattern: Reads the digits after the point as an ordinary whole number — '0.27 means twenty-seven' — so cannot map it to 27 hundredths or see its size.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Read decimals in place-value language ('twenty-seven hundredths') and locate on the hundredths grid; the two digits are 2 tenths and 7 hundredths, not the number 27.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Reads 0.27 as 'twenty-seven'; when writing 0.27 as a fraction gives something other than 27/100, or cannot place it between 0 and 1.

responseLevels.gap: Converts by copying digits regardless of place (7/100 → 0.7), or insists a decimal and its fraction are different numbers. Reads 0.27 as twenty-seven.
responseLevels.full: Writes 3/10 = 0.3, 7/100 = 0.07 with the placeholder, and 0.27 = 27/100, and explains that a decimal and its fraction name the same quantity at the same point because the places count tenths and hundredths. Handles contrasting pairs (3/10 vs 3/100) and 0.3 = 0.30, and transfers to a new value.
responseLevels.partial: Converts tenths correctly and often hundredths too, but slips on the placeholder (7/100) or can convert without explaining that the two forms are the same quantity — executes the rule without the equivalence reason.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Write 3/10 and 7/100 as decimals, and write 0.27 as a fraction. Then tell me: is 0.3 the same as 3/10, or different — and how do you know?
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: The 7/100 item exposes whether the child understands that place carries the denominator (0.07) or drops the placeholder (0.7). The tier-2 question separates a child who sees 0.3 and 3/10 as one quantity from a child who treats decimal and fraction as different kinds of number. A child converting by digit-count alone gets 3/10 right but stumbles on 7/100, revealing the rule is hollow.
